newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamist PM faces secularist wrath.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamist PM faces secularist wrath.

text.p: Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan was locked in a war of nerves with Turkey's political establishment on Thursday, one day before a meeting between top ministers and the staunchly secularist army brass.

The Hurriyet daily, a bitter critic of Erbakan, carried a front-page report of what it said was a warning from President Suleyman Demirel that the Islamist-led coalition threatened Turkey's "secularist, democratic (and) republican aims".
"If you continue with this attitude the regime will be in danger," the daily quoted the warning to Erbakan, the first Islamist leader of the officially secular republic.
Similar reports were carried in the rival Sabah newspaper. Both dailies are traditional organs of the secular political and business establishment.

Erbakan swiftly denounced the reports as "a lie", and the president's press office later denied any such letter was sent. However, the comments attributed to Demirel echo a series of recent briefings he gave to newspaper editors and columnists.

Whatever the provenance of the alleged letter, there was no doubt the reports aggravated political tensions, already running near fever pitch since the army sent tanks on manoeuvres through an Islamist suburb of the capital Ankara on February 4.
The city was rife with rumours of further sabre-rattling by the officer corps, deeply displeased by Erbakan's attempts to introduce Moslem practice into Turkish public life.
Nightly civilian protests, launched initially against state corruption, have increasingly turned against Erbakan and his Islamist Welfare Party and show little sign of dying down.
"Ankara is in confusion. Ankara is tense. Ankara is doomed to give birth to many things," commentator Ismet Berkan wrote in the daily Radikal. "Ankara is full of rumour and speculation."
Such speculation is building toward Friday's regular session of the powerful National Security Council -- a vestige of earlier military rule -- that groups senior commanders and ministers.
It is expected to issue a stern warning to Erbakan that mounting Islamist zeal threatens Turkey's secular and democratic institutions.
Few analysts, however, expect the kind of military intervention that twice before deposed then-prime minister Demirel.

"Those in Ankara who are in any way close to the military know that they have no intention of mounting a coup. They want to put pressure on the government to change its behaviour," commentator and author Mehmet Ali Birand told Reuters.
Birand, who has extensive contacts with the armed forces, suggested the soldiers might be contented if Erbakan agreed to jettison one or more of his more zealous ministers.
Financial markets, always volatile, were treading water cautiously before the Security Council session.

"Whenever such political crises are not solved within the (political) system, eyes traditionally turn to the military," said Nalan Erkarakas, general manager of Kent investment. Shares were off slightly in morning trade.
On Wednesday opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz called for an alliance of all parties except Erbakan's Welfare Party to evade the danger of the military staging a fourth coup since 1960.
